commands.review_summary:
The PR parallelizes parts of Slack inbound message preparation, removes the Slack write WebClient concurrency cap, and bounds initial thread-history pagination with focused tests.

PR surface: Source +25, Tests +42. Total +67 across 6 files.

Reproducibility: yes. source-level reproduction is high confidence: current main still has the serial prepare awaits, write cap, and unbounded thread-history pagination described by the linked issue. I did not run a live Slack workspace in this read-only review.
commands.review_followup: - [P1] Manual review is needed because the blocker is a compatibility and ordering decision around a shipped Slack write safeguard, not a safe cleanup-close or purely mechanical repair lane.

target.title: perf(slack): remove structural channel-side latency (serial prepare, global write cap, unbounded thread pagination)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #101690.

Slack replies carry a constant ~1.5–2.5s of channel-side overhead compared to Telegram/Discord on the identical agent loop. The openclaw-rtt release canaries show Slack at ~3.1–3.5s p50 on every release since the Slack canary began (vs Telegram ~1.0s, Discord ~1.8s, same `mock-openai` provider), and a production gateway on 2026.6.11 with stock socket-mode config showed a 5.1s gap between `Inbound app_mention` receipt and agent dispatch.

Three structural causes in `extensions/slack`:

1. **Serial inbound prepare chain** — `prepareSlackMessage` awaited independent Slack Web API lookups strictly sequentially (assistant-thread metadata restore, sender-name resolution for allow-name matching, thread-starter lookup), stacking cold-cache round trips before the agent is dispatched.
2. **Process-wide write serialization** — the write client pinned `maxRequestConcurrency = 1`, so every `chat.postMessage`, `chat.update` (preview/draft edits), reaction, and file-upload call on a token ran single-file across the whole process, making unrelated channels queue behind each other.
3. **Unbounded thread-history pagination** — `resolveSlackThreadHistory` walked every 200-message page of a thread oldest→newest just to keep the last N, so the first message seeding a long thread paid one serial round trip per 200 thread messages.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `perf(slack): parallelize independent inbound prepare lookups` — starts the assistant-thread restore, sender-name lookup, and thread-starter lookup at the earliest point where their inputs and gating conditions are known, and awaits them where consumed. Drop/skip/authorization semantics are unchanged: every promise starts only after the gates that could drop the message, so dropped paths gain no new API traffic, and in-flight promises settle to result objects so an early throw cannot leave an unobserved rejection. Two further overlaps were deliberately **not** taken after code inspection: `authorizeSlackInboundMessage` does not unconditionally call `users.info` (channel/app_mention and open-DM paths can skip it, so an eager entry-time lookup would add API calls those paths avoid today), and `resolveSlackMessageContent` consumes the thread starter for inherited parent-file filtering (genuinely sequential).
- `perf(slack): drop process-wide write client concurrency cap` — removes `maxRequestConcurrency ??= 1` from `resolveSlackWriteClientOptions`. Provenance: the cap came from `107d2b7a096` ("preserve rapid send ordering"); that ordering contract is now owned by the per-target `KeyedAsyncQueue` in `send.ts` (keyed `accountId:tokenHash:recipient:threadTs`), which serializes sends per conversation without serializing the whole process. Slack's ~1 msg/sec limit is per channel, not per token. `@slack/web-api` (`dist/WebClient.js`) defaults `maxRequestConcurrency` to 100 via `p-queue` and pauses/resumes the queue on 429 `Retry-After` unless `rejectRateLimitedCalls` is set, so burst safety is retained at the SDK layer. Explicit caller overrides still pass through.
- `perf(slack): bound thread history pagination` — caps `conversations.replies` history fetches at 3 pages (600 messages). Threads that fit the window keep exact last-N behavior. Slack paginates replies oldest→newest with no reverse cursor, so for longer threads the fetch returns no history (logged) instead of silently attributing stale early-thread context — deterministic, documented degradation on a pathological path.

## User Impact

Slack replies dispatch to the agent sooner (fewer serial cold-cache round trips before the turn starts) and multi-part deliveries (preview edits, reactions, chunked posts, uploads) no longer queue behind unrelated channels' writes. Long-thread cold seeding can no longer stall dispatch behind an unbounded pagination walk.

## RTT measurement (openclaw-rtt `slack-canary`, mock-openai, 20 samples/side)

Both refs measured with the same harness, credentials, runner class, and sample count (dispatched via the openclaw-rtt channel-RTT workflow with an `openclaw_ref` input):

| Ref | Samples | RTT p50 | RTT p95 | Min | Max |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| baseline `e591dcfa821` | 20/20 pass | 3,440ms | 4,802ms | 3,051ms | 4,812ms |
| fix `936f1855c4b` | 20/20 pass | 4,272ms | 4,928ms | 2,862ms | 5,527ms |

**Read this as a no-regression gate, not an improvement claim.** Both distributions are the same bimodal mixture (~3.3s and ~4.7s modes); the p50 difference is which mode samples landed in (8/20 vs 11/20 slow; Fisher p≈0.5) and within-mode medians differ by <60ms. Two harness properties cap what this scenario can resolve:

- The driver observes replies by polling (`1s sleep + conversations.history + conversations.replies` per cycle, ~1.4s effective cadence), which quantizes RTT into poll buckets — the source of the bimodality.
- The canary is a cold single-message channel mention: it never enters the thread-history, DM-history, allow-name-matching, or multi-part-delivery paths this PR changes.

### Where the canary's time actually goes (instrumented runs, 10 samples/side, per-sample SUT gateway logs + Slack server timestamps)

| Phase (p50) | baseline | fix |
|---|---:|---:|
| Slack event propagation to Socket Mode (server receipt → event arrival, zero OpenClaw code) | ~2,132ms | ~2,356ms |
| dispatch queue | 52ms | 50ms |
| agent turn (mock model) | 260ms | 249ms |
| outbound reply post | 240ms | 246ms |
| driver poll observation | ~820ms | ~890ms |

The dominant cost of Slack's RTT gap vs Telegram/Discord on this scenario is **Slack's own event delivery latency (~1.5–3.2s observed)**, which no gateway-side change can move. Total OpenClaw-controlled time (event arrival → reply posted) is under ~1s on both refs.

## Evidence

- Extension suite on Blacksmith Testbox: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/slack` — 106 files, 1476 tests, exit 0; `pnpm tsgo` exit 0.
- Repo-wide symbol sweep found no references to the removed cap outside `extensions/slack`.
- Autoreview: clean (one accepted finding during development — stale long-thread context — fixed by the no-history degradation above).
- Obsolete test asserting the removed default cap deleted; explicit-override test retained; capped-pagination path covered in `monitor/media.test.ts`.

Validation runs:

- `pnpm check:changed` lanes (remote-child) on Blacksmith Testbox: green (one initial `check:test-types` failure in the new capped-pagination test was a missing `as unknown` step in a mock cast; fixed to match the file's sibling pattern and re-verified green).
- 20-sample RTT A/B: openclaw-rtt workflow runs `28896305615` (baseline) and `28897212331` (fix); instrumented decomposition runs `28899719563` / `28899724145`.
- Branch-mode autoreview over `origin/main..HEAD`: clean, no actionable findings.

Follow-ups intentionally out of scope: the openclaw-rtt sampler's per-sample status probe still reads the pre-evidence-summary schema on its `main` (fixed on the measurement branch; separate PR to openclaw-rtt), and the canary driver's ~1.4s poll cadence limits RTT resolution.
